status.reason: At least two independent bodies of evidence agree in direction. As the claim and this morning's adjudication record them, the four adjusted studies pooled by McKetin et al. (2019) come from different groups and Boden et al. (2023) is an independent New Zealand birth cohort. Huang et al. (2022), read in full here, is a Taiwanese registry cohort whose team, country and data are separate from both. Huang's hazard ratio (5.28) is much larger than the pooled adjusted odds ratio (2.4) or Boden's 1.33. The difference has an adequate explanation (a comparison group with no drug record, minimal adjustment, claims diagnoses including a hallucination code, an arrest-defined exposure), so 'mixed' does not apply. grade.reason: Start low (observational). Risk of bias: the claim is worded as an association and rests on the adjusted pooled estimate. Huang is very high risk (ROBINS-E; I agree with the card) but does not carry the rating. Residual confounding could shrink the magnitudes, but on the evidence read it would not reverse the direction. Not downgraded. Inconsistency: not downgraded. The spread (1.33, 2.4, 5.28) follows comparator and adjustment, and the estimates are reported separately, not pooled. Indirectness: not downgraded for the claim as worded. Huang's pooling of MDMA and 21 other substances with methamphetamine is stated in the statement. No upgrade for large effect (METHODS §6.3). Huang's HR stays large under its most adjusted model, but remaining biases run away from the null: other drug and alcohol use and socio-economic position are unadjusted against a group with no drug record; there is more contact with services after arrest; and an arrest can follow a psychotic episode that is diagnosed afterwards. No upgrade for dose-response either. Arrests were counted over the whole follow-up and rise with time observed: 4.37 person-years per person with one arrest against 6.48 with five or more (recomputed). The printed trend p (0.038) is reproduced only by a regression on the five category rates (p = 0.0377; 0.070 with the zero category; 0.004 on log HRs; recomputed).

status.reason: Each of the claim's three kinds of figures rests on one body of data. The 2015-2019 survey trend rests on Han et al. (2021) alone. The death-record trend comes from three analyses of the same national death certificates: Han et al. (2021), Zhu et al. (2025), and Tanz et al. (2025), whose NVSS rates use T43.6 and whose 2023 count (34,855, cited from NCHS Data Brief 522) is the one the later analysis reports. Under METHODS §6.3 this is overlapping evidence, counted once. The SUDORS opioid share rests on Tanz et al. (2025) alone and is one pooled period, so it can show no trend and is not replicated by Han's 2019 share (different system, ages and period). A literal reading of §6.4 could call the death series 'replicated by the same team' (shared sample). But re-counting the same complete death records is not replication, and the other two parts are single studies. 'Single study' is the honest label for the claim as a whole. The claim now bundles three figures with different bases (survey 2015-2019; death records 1999-2023; SUDORS 2021-2024). Splitting it, as SENIOR-DECISIONS item 24 proposes for two other claims, would let each part carry its own exact label.

plain.proposed: In US household surveys of adults aged 18 to 64, the estimated number who said they had used meth in the past year rose by about a fifth between 2015 and 2019, and the number with a meth use disorder by about half; the surveys miss people who are homeless or in institutions. Over the same years, overdose deaths involving stimulants other than cocaine (mostly meth) nearly tripled; more than half of the 2019 deaths also involved opioids, but deaths without opioids also more than doubled. The bigger percentages often quoted from this paper start from 2016, the lowest year. Later US survey figures use different methods and are not directly comparable. Newer death records for all ages show that deaths involving meth kept rising, from about 550 in 1999 to about 35,000 in 2023, but the rise slowed after 2021 (the latest year's figures are provisional). Deaths involving both meth and fentanyl rose fastest. These newer counts come from the same death records and include all ages, so they extend the earlier figures rather than confirm them. A CDC report that used medical examiners' and toxicology reports found that meth was one of the causes of about 31 in 100 overdose deaths from 2021 to mid-2024; about 7 in 10 of those deaths also involved opioids, and about 3 in 10 did not. These reports are a different kind of record from the death records above, so this share cannot be compared directly with the 2019 one.
plain.reason: Only the Tanz sentence changes; the rest of the plain text concerns other papers and is copied unchanged. Two points. (1) 'found meth in about 31 in 100 overdose deaths' reads as detection. SUDORS counts a drug only when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death (main-text footnote §§), so 'was one of the causes' matches the measure. (2) The plain text puts '7 in 10 with opioids' (2021-2024, SUDORS) right after 'more than half of the 2019 deaths' (death certificates, ages 18-64). That invites a comparison the statement explicitly rules out ('a different system and period ... not directly comparable'). The plain text should carry that caveat, because a shallower depth must not say more than the statement (WRITING-RULES).

It calls the starting point a prediction from pre-use school grades and keeps 'No study tested people before they began to use'. Three precision points, all checked in the paper. (1) 'smoking' in the model is current adult smoking status, a post-exposure variable (34 of 37 in the methamphetamine group smoked). It lowers the group's predicted score by about 0.12 composite units (editors' calculation from the printed equation and Table 1), so 'current smoking' would be exact. (2) The model attributes about half of the group's raw gap from the controls to the predictors: predicted mean −0.30 against an actual mean of about −0.64, in the composite's units (editors' calculation; the actual mean is derived from two printed subgroup means). That is useful context for 'a decline from a higher starting point'. (3) Keep 'paired': the authors call these d values medium and 'consistent with meta-analytic data', but a paired d divides by the SD of individual shortfalls and is not on the scale of between-group d values.
